comments.author: @428ghost
comments.text:
I worked at HSC and for MB Gov until 2004 and know those tunnel systems well, as well as the U of M Fort Garry campus.  The tunnel running from the Legislature isn't as wide as stated because of the steam pipes taking up so much space.  There's a sub-basement of empty vaults under the legislature including a void under the front steps.  Very little light down there, pretty creepy.  There was a central vacuum system for that building that ran down into the basement.  If you see little brass circular plates near the floor in the hallways that's where the hoses were supposed to be plugged in.  Long since unserviceable.  I've been all the way up the tower to the Golden Boy, but my keyring didn't have the key to the last hatch where you can touch his toe.  I had photos of the various levels of vaults, but I've long since misplaced them.

The HSC tunnels used by the public have some additional hidden tunnels to service hydro vaults.  A tunnel between the School of Nursing and the Adult Psychiatric Building was sealed for years until put back in use when the new Cancer Foundation building was built.  A tunnel to the Pincock Psychiatric building was sealed for years until reconnected to the Buhler Building at the U of M.  There were rumours of a sealed tunnel running from the GC wing to where the Cancer Foundation is now, but it was likely just a service trench for a steam line.  The GC wing does have a sealed up 5th floor that would have made for a great haunted house set.  It's the oldest remaining wing in the whole complex from the 1880s if I recall.  That floor was the residence for the Chinese cooking staff as the kitchen was on the floor beneath, before the GH wing was built with the current kitchen.  The GF wing has a sealed up elevator room with the original wrought-iron elevator works and some graffiti from the early 1900s telling the tale of a love-lorn nurse who committed suicide by throwing herself off the roof.  Sadly, I've misplaced those photos as well.  There's also a hidden courtyard between the GB and GA wings that was used as a smoking area by the corporate office before the office moved.  And of course there are many sub-basements and service spaces the public and few employees see.  I had the master keys to the entire complex, I've been in every space up to 2004.

Winnipeg also has underground steams that can complicate excavations.  When the Cancer Foundation was built they hit one of them with a piling and had flooding into the foundation.  A Loss Prevention Officer who worked at the HBC building downtown said there was a sub-basement there and a stream that ran through the dirt foundation when the ground water level rose.  He also said some of the columns that were wrapped in mirrors were faux columns with one-way mirrors they'd hide in to watch for shoplifters.

replies.author: @428ghost
@HiddenCanada
replies.text: This is exactly the kind of local firsthand knowledge I was hoping people would add in the comments. You’ve mentioned several areas I never came across in the records I found, especially the old HSC connections, the Legislature sub-basements and the underground streams. The fact that you actually worked in these buildings and had access to some of these spaces adds a whole other layer to the story. Thank you for taking the time to write all of this, I may have enough here to start digging into a follow-up video.

comments.author: @StuckInPeg
comments.text:
My house on the south side of the Assiniboine River, built in 1912, still had a steam jacket on the cold side of our hydronic heating system. It supplemented heat from the coal fired (converted to gas) boiler. The steam supply pipe was sealed off by a city worker about ten years ago. There was a flow meter on the condensate pipe, to pay for the heat. District heating in 1912! Brilliant!
I had it taken out when we removed the asbestos and upgraded to a high efficiency boiler.
In winter they say you could trace the route of the steam tunnels by the melted snow.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: It’s incredible to think about that 1912 district heating system still being in use so recently; thanks for sharing that bit of local history with us! 😊

comments.author: @46babaganoosh

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Yep, the Legislature is full of different carved symbols and decorative details. That’s part of what made Frank Albo’s Hermetic Code theory so popular. The carvings are real, the debated part is whether they were deliberately arranged as one hidden symbolic system or whether later interpretations connected patterns that weren’t originally meant to form a code.
